clue.text: A long creese to dissect the fish

definitions.note: plural answer for a plural sense: a kind of fish

indicators.note: to dissect is to cut apart, so the letters of the two words are taken to pieces and reassembled

explanation.surface: Someone takes a long Malay dagger to cut up a fish.
explanation.walkthrough: A creese (kris) is a Malay dagger, which makes 'dissect' look literal. 'to dissect' rearranges LONG and CREESE.
explanation.definitionFit: These long marine eels are a familiar sea fish caught by anglers.

clue.text: Take care about wrapping a cap up in a tough casing

indicators.note: the word is put round the following pieces like a wrapping

parts.note: taking care is to care

indicators.note: in a down clue 'up' means the word is read from bottom to top, backwards

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Instructions for packing a cap carefully inside a hard case.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take care' is the verb to care, not an instruction; 'about wrapping' puts the outer word round the rest, and 'up' turns the headgear word round, as a down clue reads upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A tortoise or crab's hard shell is a protective covering.

clue.text: This will do for the present

definitions.text: This will do for the present

parts.words: This will do for the present
parts.note: the phrase 'for the …' means for now; the word fills that idiom

explanation.surface: A person settling for something adequate as a gift.
explanation.walkthrough: 'present' reads as a gift, but it is the present time: the idiom is 'for the nonce'. A nonce word is also one coined for one occasion.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means the time being, as in a word made for one occasion only.

clue.text: "O monstrous!——buckram men grown out of two" (1 Hen, IV)

definitions.text: "O monstrous!——buckram men grown out of two" (1 Hen, IV)

parts.words: "O monstrous!——buckram men grown out of two" (1 Hen, IV)
parts.note: Prince Hal mocks Falstaff, whose two attackers in buckram have multiplied in his story; the dash holds their number

explanation.surface: A quotation from Shakespeare's Henry IV Part 1 with a word left out.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash marks the gap: Falstaff's tale of robbers in buckram grows from two men to this many.
explanation.definitionFit: In Henry IV Part 1 Falstaff's two imaginary attackers swell to a number one more than ten.

parts.note: to invest a town is to besiege it, which is to surround it

explanation.surface: A tip on how to put your money to work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'invest' suggests money; its military sense is to lay siege, to encircle, and the answer is the verb to surround.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb the word means to surround or encircle, as an army invests a town.

clue.text: Make a lady run this business

indicators.note: 'Make' asks for something to be fashioned out of the letters that follow

explanation.surface: An instruction to put a woman in charge of a company.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Make' rearranges LADY and RUN.
explanation.definitionFit: A firm that washes clothes is a laundering business.

clue.text: But with no inclination towards obesity

definitions.text: But with no inclination towards obesity

parts.words: But with no inclination towards obesity
parts.note: the word for a slant or inclination also means thin and spare, so it is an inclination that leads away from fatness

explanation.surface: Someone tilts in every direction except towards getting fat.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a tilt or tendency and having no spare fat, so it names a tendency that is not towards fatness.

parts.note: the idiom for venting anger is read literally: liquid giving off vapour

explanation.surface: Someone venting their frustration.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Let off steam' is an idiom for venting feelings; read literally it is turning to vapour.
explanation.definitionFit: Water that turns to vapour gives off steam, the literal sense of the idiom.

clue.text: They, at any rate, should have wardrobes

definitions.text: They, at any rate, should have wardrobes

parts.words: They, at any rate, should have wardrobes
parts.note: 'wardrobes' splits as ward robes, the uniform of people working on hospital wards

explanation.surface: A remark that some people at least ought to own cupboards for clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wardrobes' is not furniture: read as 'ward robes', the uniforms of hospital staff who work on wards.
explanation.definitionFit: Hospital carers work on wards in uniform, so they have robes for the ward.

clue.text: Betake yourselves abroad to meet there

definitions.meaning: the French phrase literally means 'present yourselves', an order to go somewhere
the same word in English is the agreed meeting place

explanation.surface: Travellers are told to go abroad and meet up there.
explanation.definitionFit: In French the phrase is an imperative, 'betake yourselves'; borrowed into English it is a meeting place.

definitions.meaning: a young salmon in its first stage in fresh water
Catherine ... was the sixth wife of Henry VIII

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a woman called Catherine is a tiny salmon.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is a young salmon, and also the surname of Henry VIII's last queen.

definitions.meaning: a stringed instrument a little larger than the violin
the heroine of Twelfth Night, whose name is also a flower of the violet family

explanation.surface: A girl selling flowers in a musical based on Shakespeare.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is a stringed instrument, the Twelfth Night heroine and a pansy-like flower.

clue.text: You can't do better than master it

definitions.text: You can't do better than master it

parts.words: You can't do better than master it
parts.note: put 'master' in front of the answer and you get the finest work an artist can make

explanation.surface: Advice that the best thing you can do is learn a skill thoroughly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'master it' reads as 'learn it'; instead 'master' joined to the answer makes a masterwork, which cannot be bettered.
explanation.definitionFit: A piece is a work, and a master's work is the highest achievement.

parts.note: the Gilbert and Sullivan title sounds like 'ruddy gore', red blood rather than aristocratic blue blood

explanation.surface: A critic says an opera is plainly not about aristocrats.
explanation.walkthrough: Blue blood means noble birth; this Gilbert and Sullivan operetta's title suggests red gore instead.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a comic operetta by Gilbert and Sullivan, whose title reads as red blood.

parts.note: the word is a garment worn over the shoulders and also a headland standing out into the sea

explanation.surface: Smart clothing to wear on a beach holiday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outstanding' means jutting out, as a headland does from the coast; 'wear' is the sleeveless cloak.
explanation.definitionFit: It is both a sleeveless cloak and a promontory projecting into the sea.

clue.text: Rhymester trying the Cask of Amontillado ?

parts.note: Edgar Allan Poe wrote the story 'The Cask of Amontillado'
a taster is one who tries food or drink

explanation.surface: A poet sampling a famous sherry cask.
explanation.walkthrough: The Cask of Amontillado is a story by Edgar Allan Poe, so trying it makes one a taster of Poe.
explanation.definitionFit: A poetaster is a writer of trivial verse, a mere versifier.

parts.note: Hamlet tells his mother that his black garment alone cannot show his grief

explanation.surface: A remark on the black clothes Hamlet wears in grief.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Habit' could be a custom, but here it is clothing: Hamlet's line ''Tis not alone my inky cloak, good mother'.
explanation.definitionFit: Hamlet calls his black mourning garment this in Act 1 Scene 2.

parts.note: Hamlet's first line; the gap holds the missing word

explanation.surface: A quotation with a word left out.
explanation.walkthrough: Hamlet's aside on his uncle: 'A little more than kin, and less than kind'.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word means relatives, family by blood or marriage, as Claudius is to Hamlet.

parts.note: the name splits as the French article and the English article, so it says 'the' in two languages

explanation.surface: A river whose name works in two languages.
explanation.walkthrough: The underworld river of forgetfulness in Greek myth: its name reads as French 'le' plus English 'the'.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the river of oblivion in Hades, and its letters are 'the' in French then English.

parts.note: a cottage loaf is a traditional British loaf shape, so these homes would suit loaves, not idle people

explanation.surface: Housing for retired layabouts.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'loafer' sounds like an idler, but a cottage loaf is an old-style British loaf made of two rounds stacked.
explanation.definitionFit: Small country houses are homes, and the cottage loaf is named after them.

parts.note: 'part' is a verb, to separate, and the noun is the act of separating

explanation.surface: Something only partly carried out, like a half-finished operation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Part' looks like 'partial'; it is the verb 'to part', and the answer is the operation of parting.
explanation.definitionFit: Severing is cutting apart, so this noun is the act of parting things.

clue.text: Its customers are a flighty lot

definitions.text: Its customers are a flighty lot

parts.words: Its customers are a flighty lot
parts.note: 'flighty' means capricious but also taking flights

explanation.surface: A shop whose customers are fickle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flighty' suggests fickle; its customers literally take flights.
explanation.definitionFit: A company that carries passengers by aeroplane has flying customers.

parts.note: the idiom for an ambitious opportunist is read as someone who makes things

explanation.surface: An ambitious, self-seeking person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On the make' means out for gain; read literally it describes a maker.
explanation.definitionFit: One who makes or brings things into being is a maker.

clue.text: Where to go in the States in the forenoon

definitions.text: Where to go in the States

indicators.note: the second 'in' says the answer lies inside the words that follow it

explanation.surface: Travel advice on which American place to visit in the morning.
explanation.walkthrough: The Nevada city was famous for quick divorces, so it is 'where to go' in the US. The second 'in' signals the hidden word in forenoon.
explanation.definitionFit: This Nevada city is a destination in the United States, once known for quick divorces.

parts.note: three is an odd number, and the phrase completed with 'out' names the one left over

explanation.surface: A batsman third in the order is dismissed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Number three' sounds like a batting position; three is odd, so the 'odd man' goes out, giving 'odd man out'.
explanation.definitionFit: The odd man out is the one left over in a group, as three is odd.

indicators.note: perverted means twisted out of its proper form, so the word's letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Twisting facts to gain approval.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perverted' rearranges TRUTHS. 'go-ahead' here is drive or push rather than permission.
explanation.definitionFit: Thrust is forward drive or push, a go-ahead force.

clue.text: Backyard clothes-dryer, for example of H.P.

indicators.note: 'Back' set before 'yard' says that word is to be read in reverse

parts.note: a clothes horse is a wooden frame on which washing is dried

explanation.surface: A clothes airer in the back yard, offered as some example of hire purchase.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backyard' looks like one place but splits into a reversal signal and its word. H.P. is horsepower, not hire purchase, so a working horse is an example of it.
explanation.definitionFit: Horsepower is power supplied by horses, and this heavy cart animal is one source of it.

clue.text: Male item in a slave market?

definitions.text: Male item in a slave market?

parts.note: a male person is a he
a lot is an item put up at an auction

explanation.surface: A man put up for sale at a slave auction.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines the answer: a Spartan serf, which here is a he sold as an auction lot.
explanation.definitionFit: A helot was a serf of ancient Sparta, a man in bondage like a slave.

definitions.meaning: the zodiac sign of the scales
the pound sign comes from the Latin for a pound weight

explanation.surface: An account balance of one pound.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the Latin for scales, the zodiac sign, and the pound from which £ is drawn.

definitions.meaning: a South American herbal infusion drunk from a gourd

explanation.surface: Looking for someone to share a cup of tea with.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means a friend and is also the South American herbal infusion.

parts.note: the mint is where coins are made
humbug is nonsense or deceptive talk

explanation.surface: A cynic calls the business of making money pleasant nonsense.
explanation.walkthrough: A HUMBUG is a traditional British boiled sweet, striped and often peppermint flavoured.
explanation.definitionFit: This striped peppermint boiled sweet is a classic British confection.

clue.text: Just the girl to "cut the painter "?

definitions.text: Just the girl to "cut the painter

parts.words: Just the girl to "cut the painter
parts.note: to cut the painter is to cut a boat's mooring rope and break free; Ibsen's heroine walks out on her husband

explanation.surface: A woman likely to snub an artist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Painter' is not an artist but a boat's rope. Ibsen's heroine of A Doll's House leaves her home and husband at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Ibsen's heroine in A Doll's House breaks her ties and leaves her marriage.

clue.text: The last bother, perhaps, of single folk

definitions.text: The last bother, perhaps, of single folk

indicators.note: 'perhaps' says the words given may be shaped differently, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: Engagements are the final worry of people who are still unmarried.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' signals the rearrangement, and the whole clue describes engagements as the final trouble people face before they stop being single.
explanation.definitionFit: Engagements to marry are the last stage of being unwed.
